Circulation of Rickettsia species and rickettsial endosymbionts
among small mammals and their ectoparasites in Eastern Slovakia
Eva Špitalská1 & Jasna Kraljik2 & Dana Miklisová3 & Eva Boldišová1 & Olivier A. E. Sparagano4 & Michal Stanko2,3
Received: 2 December 2019 /Accepted: 28 April 2020
Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2020
Abstract
Bacteria belonging to the genus Rickettsia are known as causative agents of vector-borne zoonotic diseases, such as spotted
fevers, epidemic typhus and endemic typhus. Different species of ticks, mites and fleas could act as reservoirs and arthropod
vectors of different pathogenic Rickettsia species. The aim of this work was to establish active surveillance of Rickettsia spp. in
mites, ticks and fleas collected from small mammals (rodents and shrews) in Eastern Slovakia. A total of 964 animal ear biopsies,
871 mites, 667 ticks and 743 fleas were collected from small mammals in the Košice region, Eastern Slovakia. All specimens
were identified using specialized taxonomic keys, and were conserved in ethanol until DNA extraction was performed. After
DNA extraction, identification of Rickettsia species was performed by PCR-based methods. The total prevalence of rickettsiae
from ear biopsies was
CI, 3.2–5.9), in tested mites
CI, 14.3–20.1) in I. ricinus
ticks and
CI, 2.2–4.8) in fleas. Sequence analysis of the partial gltA gene and Rickettsia helvetica-, Rickettsia
slovaca-, Rickettsia raoultii- species specific real-time PCR tests revealed the presence of R. helvetica, R. slovaca, unidentified
Rickettsia and rickettsial endosymbionts. These pathogenic and symbiotic species were confirmed in the following ectoparasite
species—Laelaps jettmari, Haemogamasus nidi, Laelaps agilis and Eulaelaps stabularis mites, Ixodes ricinus ticks,
Ctenophthalmus solutus, C. assimilis and Megabothris turbidus fleas infesting host—Apodemus agrarius, A. flavicollis,
Microtus arvalis and Myodes glareolus small mammals. These results confirm the circulation of R. helvetica, R. slovaca,
unidentified Rickettsia and rickettsial endosymbionts in mites, ticks and fleas collected on small mammals in the Košice region,
Eastern Slovakia.

Introduction
A wide range of mammals, including rodents, act as reservoir
hosts and can participates in the natural cycle of several zoo-
notic agents. They play an important role in the circulation of
hantaviruses (Klempa et al. 2005), agents of larval toxocarosis
(Antolová et al. 2004; Reiterová et al. 2013), leptospirosis
(Stanko et al. 1996), chlamydiosis (Čisláková et al. 2004),
borreliosis (Hanincová et al. 2003), anaplasmosis (Blaňarová
et al. 2014), bartonellosis (Kraljik et al. 2016), babesiosis
(Blaňarová et al. 2016) and other zoonosis (Čondlová et al.
2018; Danišová et al. 2017; Mácová et al. 2018). Small mam-
mals are hosts to different ectoparasites such as ticks (Nosek
et al. 1972; Labuda et al. 1989; Krasnov et al. 2007, 2010),
mites (Kocianová 1980; Stanko 1989), fleas (Rosický 1957;
Stanko et al. 2002; Krasnov et al. 2006, 2010) and lice (Stanko
et al. 2015). Several small mammals such as Apodemus
flavicollis (Melchior, 1834), Apodemus agrarius (Pallas,

1771), Myodes glareolus (Schreber, 1780), Microtus arvalis
(Pallas, 1778), Microtus subterraneus (de Sélys-Longchamps,
1836), Micromys minutus (Pallas, 1771) and Sorex araneus
(Linnaeus, 1758) have a relevant epidemiological role as hosts
to a broad spectrum of ectoparasites mentioned above in
Slovakia (Meerburg et al. 2009; Špitalská et al. 2015, 2017;
Minichová et al. 2017).
Ticks are obligate ectoparasites that feed on a wide range of
mammalian, avian and reptilian hosts. In Europe, changes in
tick occurrence are observed as a result of climatic changes,
economic and socio-economic conditions. Such changes re-
sults in the establishment of new foci and the spread of vector-
borne diseases (Bullová et al. 2009; Lukáň et al. 2010). Five
genera and 21 species of soft and hard ticks were recognized
in different fauna of Slovakia (Slovák 2010) from which epi-
demiologically important species belonging to Ixodes ricinus
Linnaeus 1758; Haemaphysalis concinna Koch 1844;
Haemaphysalis punctata Canestrini & Fanzago, 1878;
Haemaphysalis inermis Birula, 1895; Dermacentor
reticulatus Fabricius, 179; and Dermacentor marginatus
Sulzer, 1776. Ixodes ricinus collected from vegetation and
animals in different locations of Slovakia were previously
found to be infected with Rickettsia helvetica and Rickettsia
monacensis (Minichová et al. 2017; Radzijevskaja et al. 2015;
Špitalská et al. 2014, 2016, 2018; Švehlová et al. 2014), and
Dermacentor species with Rickettsia slovaca and Rickettsia
raoultii (Švehlová et al. 2014; Špitalská et al. 2012, 2018).
The genus Rickettsia includes obligate intracellular Gram-
negative bacteria that are responsible for mild to severe dis-
eases in humans, with worldwide distribution (Raoult and
Roux 1997). The Rickettsia species (Proteobacteria:
Rickettsiales) found in Slovakia are pathogenic to humans
(Uchiyama 2012; Oteo and Portillo 2012) with mild clinical
manifestations such as fever, rash and eschar with different
severities (Faccini-Martínez et al. 2014).
About 75 species of fleas (Siphonaptera) have been record-
ed in Slovakia, while more than 30 species were reported from
small mammals (Cyprich et al. 2002; Dudich 1993; Rosický
1957; Stanko et al. 2002). Fleas play a role in maintaining and
transferring several pathogenic agents such as Bartonella
henselae causing cat scratch disease and other Bartonella spe-
cies (Brinkerhoff et al. 2010; Marie et al. 2006; Morick et al.
2009, 2010). The oriental rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) is pri-
marily the vector of Rickettsia typhi and transmits murine
typhus to humans. Interestingly, some other species of fleas,
including the cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis), have been found
to be naturally infected with R. typhi (Azad and Beard 1998).
In Slovakia, the role of fleas in the circulation of rickettsiae is
still not well understood. To this day, Rickettsia felis and
Rickettsia africae were detected in Slovakia (Sekeyová et al.
2012; Špitalská et al. 2015). Rickettsia felis was identified in
Ctenophthalmus solutus collected from A. agrarius. The cat
flea, Ctenocephalides felis, is known as the primary vector of
R. felis, which is the etiological agent of the flea-borne spotted
fever with clinical symptoms similar to malaria and dengue in
humans. However, it appears to be milder than other
rickettsioses (Raoult and Parola 2007). R. africae was identi-
fied in Ceratophyllus garei fleas collected from reed warblers
(Acrocephalus scirpaceus) migrating from Africa (Sekeyová
et al. 2012), However, R. africae is usually transmitted by
ticks.
Mites have a broad range of eating habits. In fact, they
occupy every feeding niche-from predators, phytophagous,
decomposers and fungivores (e.g. oribatid mites, or some
mesostigmatic mites) to scavengers or parasites of other ani-
mals (Badiertakis et al. 2014). Mites of the family Laelapidae
(Acari: Mesostigmata) are distributed worldwide and are the
most common ectoparasites of small rodents (Guo et al. 2013;
Karg 1971, 1993; Kocianová 1989; Mašán and Fenďa 2010;
Miťková et al. 2015; Rynkiewicz et al. 2013). Mesostigmatic
mites are probably involved in the circulation of some patho-
gens such as the human pathogenic tick-borne encephalitis
virus or various rickettsial agents (Kocianová et al. 1993;
Miťková et al. 2015; Radzijevskaja et al. 2018; Reeves et al.
2006). The mites of the genus Allodermanyssus may act as a
vector and reservoir of Rickettsia akari, which produced urban
outbreaks, with the house mouse Mus musculus as the main
host for this mite species (Raoult and Roux 1997).
Ectoparasitic mites, fleas and ticks share the body of the
mammalian host, and by co-feeding, some uninfected para-
sites can become infected. In this study, we aimed to investi-
gate the presence and prevalence of Rickettsia species and
rickettsial endosymbionts in ectoparasites parasitizing small
mammals in Slovakia. We predicted (i) the presence of
Rickettsia species in all studied ectoparasites with the highest
prevalence in ticks, (ii) a higher prevalence in the most abun-
dant small mammals species carrying such ectoparasites and
(iii) the identification of several rickettsial species.

DNA extraction and molecular analysis
Ectoparasites were washed with sterile water, dried, trans-
ferred to individual tubes and crushed with a sterile carbon
steel surgical scalpel blade (Surgeon, JAI Surgicals Ltd.,
India). Total DNA of fleas and mites was isolated by boiling
individual specimen in
0 . 7 \textbf { M }
ammonium hydroxide
(Rijpkema et al. 1996). Genomic DNA from fed ticks and
rodent tissues were extracted using DNeasy Blood and
Tissue Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s recommen-
dations. The quantity and quality of DNA were assessed with
a NanoPhotometer Pearl (Implen, Germany). DNA samples
were stored at
- 2 0 { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
and later used as templates for the PCR
amplifications. Ectoparasite and tissue samples were screened
by PCR-based methods for the presence of Rickettsia spp.
Identification of Rickettsia spp. was performed using a nested
PCR based on the genus-specific variable regions of the gltA
gene using the primer sets
\mathrm { R p C S . 8 7 7 p - R p C S . 1 2 5 8 n }
and
RpCS.896p–RpCS.1233n (Choi et al. 2005; Regnery et al.
1991). The DNAs from Rickettsia-free ticks and nuclease-
free water were used as negative controls for each reaction
set. DNAs of R. slovaca and R. helvetica originated from the
sample bank of the Institute of Virology BMC SAS Bratislava
were used as positive controls. PCR amplifications were con-
ducted using SuperHot Master Mix (Bioron, Germany) as
recommended by the manufacturer using a thermocycler
Labcycler (SensoQuest, Germany). PCR products were ana-
lyzed by electrophoresis in a
agarose gel, stained with
GelRed™ (Biotium, Hayward, California) and visualized
with a UV transilluminator. Some Rickettsia-positive samples
were screened for the presence of R. helvetica, R. slovaca and
R. raoultii species using a TaqMan PCR assay targeting a
fragment of the 23S rRNA and ompB genes, respectively, as
previously described (Boretti et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2012).
Randomly selected amplicons of gltA gene were purified and
analyzed by sequencing both DNA strands. The sequencing
was performed by Macrogen (http://www.macrogen.com).
Obtained DNA sequences were compared with available

sequences in the GenBank database using the basic local
alignment search tool (BLAST) on http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.
gov/. A phylogenetic analysis was further performed using the
MEGA5 software (Tamura et al. 2011).

Chi-square and Fisher’s tests were used to analyze the preva-
lence levels for significant independence (http://www.

Results
A total of 964 ear biopsies, 871 mites, 667 ticks and 743 fleas
were analyzed individually for the presence of rickettsial spe-
cies. Ear samples originated from the following rodents spe-
cies: A. agrarius, A. flavicollis, My. glareolus, M. arvalis,
M. subterraneus and Mi. minutus, and following insectivores:
Crocidura suaveolens Pallas, 1811; Neomys fodiens Pennant,
1771; and Sorex minutus Linnaeus, 1776 and S. araneus.
From the trapped small mammals, we identified the following
mite species: Laelaps agilis, Koch, 1836; Laelaps jettmari,
Vitzthum, 1930; Laelaps hilaris, Koch, 1836; Androlaelaps
fahrenholzi (Berlese, 1911); Hyperlaelaps microti, Ewing,

Discussion
Small mammals are important hosts for immature stages of
ticks and are considered reservoir hosts for some tick-borne
pathogens, such as tick-borne encephalitis virus, Borrelia
afzelii, Borrelia garinii, Borrelia miyamotoi, Babesia microti
and Anaplasma phagocytophilum (Randolph et al. 1999;
Humair et al. 1999; Huegli et al. 2002; Burri et al. 2014;
Parasitol Res
Springer
Obiegala et al. 2015). Evaluating the role of rodents in rick-
ettsia life cycles has been the subject of many studies (Sprong
et al. 2009; Svoboda et al. 2014; Miťková et al. 2015;
Špitalská et al. 2015; Obiegala et al. 2016; Minichová et al.
2017). In this study, we showed the presence and the molec-
ular characterization of the following rickettsial species:
R. helvetica, R. slovaca, unidentified Rickettsia and rickettsial
endosymbionts in eight species of ectoparasites, tick, fleas or
mites, (L. jettmari, H. nidi, L. agilis, E. stabularis, I. ricinus,
C. solutus, C. assimilis and M. turbidus) infesting four species
of small mammals (A. agrarius, A. flavicollis, M. arvalis and
My. glareolus) circulating in the Košice region, Eastern
Slovakia. Considering the trophic relationships related to
small mammals, two mite species, L. jettmari and L. agilis,
are considered obligatory parasites living all their cycle on the
body of rodents. The next two species, H. nidi and
E. stabularis, represent facultative hematophagous parasites,
in their life cycle with alternately living conditions in nests and
on the host bodies (Mašán and Fenďa 2010). For fleas, only
C. assimilis has stronger trophic relationships to M. arvalis or
other microtid rodents. The next two rickettsia positive flea
species, C. solutus and M. turbidus, infest a broader host spec-
trum of rodents including the Apodemus, Myodes, Microtus
and Micromys genera (Rosický 1957). Similarly broad host
parasitism is common in I. ricinus ticks (Fillipova, 1977).
We reported the highest rickettsial infection in I. ricinus ticks
followed by mites, and the lowest was recorded in fleas. A
similar study was conducted in Lithuania by Radzijevskaja
et al. (2018); ectoparasites collected from rodents were inves-
tigated for the presence of Rickettsia spp. They found the
highest infection in fleas, followed by I. ricinus ticks and then
mites. Results suggest that different vectors share small mam-
mals as reservoir hosts and rickettsia-positive ectoparasites
could be infected by the acquisition of bacteria via blood
meals from rickettsiemic hosts, or by co-feeding of ectopara-
sites through infected blood meals. They could be also infect-
ed during previous feedings on another host. Furthermore,
positive larvae could be the result of transovarial transmission
from infected females or through transstadial transmission
passed onto the next developmental stages.
Rickettsial species in ticks in Slovakia have been studied
during the last decade, and the presence of R. helvetica and
R. slovaca in I. ricinus and Dermacentor spp. was previously
confirmed (Špitalská et al. 2018) and thus expected in ticks
from this study. R. helvetica was confirmed not only in
I. ricinus ticks but also in L. jettmari, H. nidi and L. agilis mite
species and C. solutus and M. turbidus flea species.
Previously, R. helvetica was identified in C. agyrtes males
collected from A. agrarius, which was for the first time, it
was identified in fleas from Slovakia in 2015 (Špitalská
et al. 2015). Similarly, Sprong et al. (2009) identified
R. helvetica in fleas isolated from My. glareolus and
Apodemus sylvaticus from the Netherlands. R. helvetica was
also identified in Archaeopsylla erinacei collected from
hedgehogs and in Nycteridopsylla eusarca bat fleas from
Hungary (Hornok et al. 2012, 2014). The presence of
R. helvetica in pooled samples of L. agilis, H. nidi
(Laelapidae), Hirsutiella zachvatkini and Kepkatrombicula
štorkáni (Trombiculidae) mites collected from small terrestrial
mammals captured in south-western Slovakia was confirmed

by Miťková et al. (2015). Radzijevskaja et al. (2018) men-
tioned the presence of R. helvetica in I. ricinus ticks, in
L. agilis and M. gigas mites and in C. agyrtes, M. turbidus
and M. walkeri fleas.
The natural known vectors of R. slovaca are Dermacentor
species ticks, and in this study, such pathogen was confirmed
in L. agilis, L. jettmari and E. stabularis, which shows that it
can be acquired from other hosts. Previously, R. slovaca was
identified in I. ricinus in Austria (Schőtta et al. 2017) and in
Melophagus ovinus, the sheep ked in China (Liu et al. 2016).
The presence of unidentified Rickettsia species or rickettsial
endosymbiont in different species of ectoparasites has been
recorded in many studies (Blair et al. 2004; Khrouf et al.
2014; Segura et al. 2014; Song et al. 2018), and it could be
result of mis-identity with multiple Rickettsia species, unsuc-
cessful amplification of other genes, low DNA quantity used
for other amplifications, low quality of DNA, as usually the
isolate is not obtained by culture, thus the characterization is
not complete and the amount of DNA based on what is col-
lected and extracted.
The low prevalence of Rickettsia in skin biopsies was ex-
pected, as suggested by the previous study of Minichová et al.
(2017). The presence of different rickettsial species was ex-
pected. However, we expected also the presence of
R. monacensis because this species has been identified in pre-
vious studies from Slovakia, Lithuania and Italy (Špitalská
et al. 2014, Špitalská et al. 2016, Minichová et al. 2017,
Radzijevska et al. 2018, Mori et al. 2018). We assumed that
no identification of R. monacensis could be caused by not all
positive samples were sequenced and partially due to
the competition with the most prevalent R. helvetica in
Slovakia (Švehlová et al. 2014; Špitalská et al. 2014;
Špitalská et al. 2016).
Finally, the present data extend the knowledge on the dis-
tribution of Rickettsia spp. and their association with different
arthropod vectors and indicate the presence of phylogenetical-
ly distinct rickettsiae in multiple ectoparasite species
feeding on different rodent hosts. Results confirmed
the high circulation of bacteria from the genus
Rickettsia in mites, ticks and fleas collected from small
mammals in Košice region, Eastern Slovakia, with relat-
ed clinical cases of rickettsiosis. Some mite, flea and
tick species infesting wild rodents might carry Rickettsia spe-
cies, and small mammals can serve as carriers of Rickettsia
infected ectoparasites.
Conclusions
We are reporting here the occurrence and molecular charac-
terization of Rickettsia spp. in eight species of ectoparasites
found on four species of small rodents in Eastern Slovakia.
The data presented in this paper extend the knowledge on the
distribution of Rickettsia species, their association with differ-
ent arthropod vectors and rodent-parasites interactions.
